analysis.one_liner: Raises minimum fines for mine safety violations and makes operators pay penalties before appealing.
analysis.headline: Senator Durbin's bill to raise minimum mine safety fines and require faster payment drew no cosponsors and died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977 to set a $500 minimum fine for every safety violation, replacing a $250 cap on certain penalties. It would have required mine operators to pay a fine promptly, before challenging it before the review commission or in court, instead of being able to hold the money during appeals. It also directed the Labor Department to report annually to Congress on fines assessed versus fines actually collected, posting the report online, and doubled the authorized funding for federal health and safety grants to states from $10 million to $20 million [S2][S3]. It was introduced in March 2006, referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and never moved again before that Congress ended [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Miners and their families benefit from stronger financial consequences for operators who violate safety standards. The record shows how: every violation would carry at least a $500 fine [S3], operators would have to pay penalties before contesting them rather than keeping the money through years of appeal [S3], and Congress and the public would see each year how much in fines companies were assessed versus actually paid [S3]. The Labor Department would also have doubled authorized funds for state-level mine health and safety programs [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Sets a minimum $500 civil penalty for any violation of a mine health or safety standard, and replaces a $250 maximum on a class of penalties with a flat $500 [S3].

Requires operators to promptly pay a civil penalty after it is assessed and before they can contest it before the Federal Mine Safety and Health Review Commission or appeal to court, closing a delay that let companies hold disputed money while cases dragged on [S3].

Requires the Secretary of Labor to report to Congress each year on the amount of fines assessed from and actually collected by each operator, and to post the report prominently on the Labor Department website [S3].
Raises the authorization for federal health and safety grants to states from $10 million to $20 million per year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mine operators would pay more per violation and would have to pay before appealing, weakening their cash and leverage in penalty disputes. The federal government would bear up to $10 million more per year in authorized grant spending, and state programs would gain matching administrative work. These costs were never imposed, because the bill did not pass.

drawbacks.text: A $500 minimum fine is small money to a large mining company, so even supporters had to acknowledge it changes behavior at the margins rather than transforming enforcement; the bill's real teeth were the pay-before-appeal rule and public reporting, not the penalty size [S3].

Requiring operators to pay penalties before contesting them creates a cash-flow burden for small independent mines, which would have to front money for fines they might legitimately win back on appeal [S3].
Doubling the state grant authorization adds federal spending, and annual per-operator reporting adds administrative work for the Labor Department [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to miner safety were modest but real and cheap: higher minimum fines, faster collection, and public visibility into who pays what. The costs fall on mine operators and on federal grant spending. An honest supporter would concede the $500 floor is small relative to the industry's scale, but the bill was a narrow, low-cost tightening of an existing law, and there is no evidence in the record of opposition to its substance; it simply never moved.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate HELP Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on March 16, 2006 and spoke about it on the Senate floor; it was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors in the Senate [S4].
The committee took no further action; the bill's action history ends with the referral, and it died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mine operators came out better off: no higher minimum fines, no requirement to pay penalties before appeal, and no new public reporting on assessed versus collected fines. The small state grant increase was never authorized either. Miners gained nothing because the protections were never enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mine operators, whose fines stayed as they were

for.name: Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor; he was its only sponsor.

against.name: Michael Enzi
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; the committee held no hearing or markup on it, and it never came to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator, a Democrat, sponsored the bill and no senator of either party cosponsored it, so it never generated a recorded vote from which to read a party split [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have raised minimum fines per safety violation and required operators to pay penalties before appealing, ending their ability to hold disputed money during lengthy contests. Operators' interest in keeping fines low and delaying payment runs against miners' interest in safety enforcement, though the costs were modest in dollar terms.
